lesson_title: Variables and Data Types in C++

lesson_plan.overview: Teaches the four fundamental C++ data types, int, float, char, bool, with actual memory sizes, stack addresses, and live examples showing how to declare, initialize, and print variables.
lesson_plan.hook: Every program that has ever run, from a calculator to a game, stores data in variables. Today you will see exactly what happens in memory when you write int x = 42 in C++.

segments.text: Every program that has ever run stores data in variables. Today you will see exactly what happens in memory when you write int x equals 42 in C plus plus.
A variable is a named location in memory. In C plus plus you must declare its type before using it. The type tells the compiler how many bytes to reserve and how to interpret those bytes.

C plus plus has four fundamental data types you will use constantly. int stores whole numbers using 4 bytes. float stores decimal numbers using 4 bytes. char stores a single character using 1 byte. And bool stores true or false using 1 byte.

When you declare a local variable it goes onto the stack. The stack grows downward in memory. So if you declare int x first, then int y, then y will be at a lower address than x. Each variable sits at a fixed address during its lifetime.

Here is how to declare, initialize, and print all four types. Include iostream for cout. In main, declare an int named age set to 25. A float named price set to 9.99. A char named grade set to A. And a bool named passed set to true. Then print each one with cout.
The sizeof operator is your best tool for understanding memory. sizeof int returns 4 on any 64-bit system. sizeof char always returns 1. These sizes are guaranteed by the C plus plus standard.

Quick recap. You learned four core types: int, float, char, and bool. Each has a fixed byte size. Local variables live on the stack. Use sizeof to verify memory usage at compile time. Next lesson: arithmetic operators and type conversions.

int y declared second → address 0x7ffe…a0 (4 bytes lower)
All local variables are freed when the function returns
